title: When classical physics ran out of answers
description: The glow of hot objects broke the physics of 1900: students read black-body curves, meet the ultraviolet catastrophe and Planck's energy packets, and explore a timeline of modern physics with short biographies.

sources.title: Lord Kelvin (Wikipedia): the lecture 'Nineteenth-Century Clouds over the Dynamical Theory of Heat and Light', Royal Institution, 27 April 1900; the misattributed 'nothing new to be discovered' quote
Heinrich Hertz (Wikipedia): Maxwell's theory 1864, Hertz's experiments 1886–1889
Black-body radiation (Wikipedia): Kirchhoff's term 'black body' (1860), Stefan 1879, filament lamps about 2700 K
Wien's displacement law (Wikipedia): Wien 1893, b = 2.897771955 · 10⁻³ m·K, the Sun's peak near 500 nm, skin near 10 µm
Rayleigh–Jeans law (Wikipedia): Rayleigh's derivation of June 1900, the complete derivations of 1905 by Rayleigh and Jeans
Ultraviolet catastrophe (Wikipedia): the term first used by Paul Ehrenfest in 1911
Planck's law (Wikipedia): Lummer and Pringsheim, Rubens and Kurlbaum, Planck's law presented on 19 October 1900
Heinrich Rubens (Wikipedia): long-wavelength measurements at the Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt in Berlin, 7 October 1900
Max Planck (Wikipedia): the quantum hypothesis presented to the German Physical Society on 14 December 1900, 'an act of despair'
Planck constant and Boltzmann constant: exact SI values since 2019 (h = 6.62607015 · 10⁻³⁴ J·s, k_B = 1.380649 · 10⁻²³ J/K)
Fotoni material bank, University of Helsinki: the station 'thermal radiation and black-body radiation' measures the spectrum of a filament
